>Um, how many edges are there?

One.

> It makes it sound singular some times, but makes it sound plural other
> times.  If it is singular, what happens when two people should get it?

This never occurs.  You can get The Edge as a result of a succesful
bleed, or a political action.

Anytime anyone bleeds anyone else, they get The Edge -- even if
someone else had it.  It's very hard to hold on to (but the extra
blood is worth the effort).

If a political card grants someone The Edge as a result of a vote,
again, it's taken away from whoever has it at the moment.

If the card has an action icon on it, it's neccesary.  A Bleed action
is one without a card.  When you play a Computer Hacking card, you're
not taking a Bleed action, you're taking a "Computer Hacking" action
the consequence of which is a bleed.  So the (D) really is neccesary.

If it were an Action Modifier, this wouldn't be the case.

About threat counters...

WHEN can you give up The Edge to get rid of a threat counter?  It's
not specified in the rules anywhere I've seen.

If you say "at any time", then the moment it's obvious a bleed is
going to be succesful, people will give it up.  That's unfair -- the
person giving up The Edge was going to lose it *anyway*.

I'd like it to be:
1) When you first acquire the edge, you can immediately give it up,
2) When you first get a reason to give up the edge (eg. acquire a
   threat counter), you can immediately give it up, and
3) At the end of your turn (during your discard phase) you can give it up.

What was the intent of the original authors?

Messages.Author: Tom Wylie
Messages.Body:
Doug  Dejulio <ddj+@pitt.edu> wrote:
>WHEN can you give up The Edge to get rid of a threat counter?  It's
>not specified in the rules anywhere I've seen.
>If you say "at any time", then the moment it's obvious a bleed is
>going to be succesful, people will give it up.  That's unfair -- the
>person giving up The Edge was going to lose it *anyway*.

If they hang onto the Edge there are two situations:

1.  That player only has one threat counter.  Thus the threat and the
Edge offset each other in terms of the blood pool.  Basically, the person
is hanging onto the Edge to get a vote at some point, and if they do
use it for a vote, then the threat won't have anything to offset its
loss, and they'll start losing pool again every turn.  It does provide a
deterrent to being hit with more Sabbat Threats, though, since the
second one will be "useless".

2.  That player has two threat counters, and thus will be losing pool
every turn.  Again, the only benefit from hanging onto the edge is to
get a vote at some point, but in this case it's almost certainly a bad
idea to do so, since you're constantly losing blood in the meantime, and
will be back to losing it twice as fast once you do vote with the Edge.

IMHO, if they want to get a vote in exchange for long-term loss of
pool, they're welcome to it.  I don't think is this particularly more
"fair" or "unfair" than using the Edge to make a Regaining the Upper
Hand vote fail ("if I can't have it, no one will!")  Keeping the edge
rather than getting rid of threat counters just isn't buying them anything.
While I'll ask about this, I strongly suspect you're free to trade in
the Edge at any time.


Tom Wylie		rec.games.deckmaster Network Representative for
aahz@hal.com			Wizards of the Coast, Inc.

Umm, Doug, I believe Tom was refering to a card called "Sabbat Threat."  It's
a political action that gives players "Threat Counters."  Every turn you
have a threat counter on you, you lose a blood from your pool.  Should
this action be taken (and not blocked) and the vote passes, the only
remaining way to lose the counter it may create is to give up the Edge.
Threat counters have nothing to do with being bleed.  (While it is a threat,
and you would like to counter it, it's not quite the same.)  Yet another
victim the the brilliantly (sic) written rules.  Still, if you can
conprehend the rules (requiring a PhD in Astrophysics) the game is fun.

"Tragic Love Affair" can be burned by giving up The Edge.  You'll have
the situation of someone who is keeping The Edge to gain blood, but
decides when someone else takes it, "if I'm going to lose it anyway, I
may as well get rid of the Tragic Love Affair".

Mostly Harmless [Alan De Smet] <chaos@picard.cs.wisc.edu> wrote:
>Doug  Dejulio <ddj+@pitt.edu> wrote:
>>About threat counters...
>>
>>WHEN can you give up The Edge to get rid of a threat counter?  It's
>>not specified in the rules anywhere I've seen.
>>
>>If you say "at any time", then the moment it's obvious a bleed is
>>going to be succesful, people will give it up.  That's unfair -- the
>>person giving up The Edge was going to lose it *anyway*.
>
>Umm, Doug, I believe Tom was refering to a card called "Sabbat Threat."  It's
>a political action that gives players "Threat Counters."  Every turn you
>have a threat counter on you, you lose a blood from your pool.  Should
>this action be taken (and not blocked) and the vote passes, the only
>remaining way to lose the counter it may create is to give up the Edge.
>Threat counters have nothing to do with being bleed.  (While it is a threat,
>and you would like to counter it, it's not quite the same.)  Yet another
>victim the the brilliantly (sic) written rules.  Still, if you can
>conprehend the rules (requiring a PhD in Astrophysics) the game is fun.

I understand what Tom was talking about exactly.  You didn't
understand me.  Let me be more explicit.

We were playing a multiplayer game.  A Sabbat Threat vote passed.
Player "Moe" got a threat counter.  Plater "Moe" also had The Edge.
He held on to it.

Later, player "Larry" had his turn.  Player "Larry" decided to bleed
player "Curly".  "Curly" tried to block, and "Larry" played a +stealth
action modifier.  Now, if "Larry" succeeds in bleeding "Curly",
"Larry" will get The Edge and "Moe" won't have it any more.  So, AT
THIS TIME, "Moe" decided to give up The Edge to destroy a threat
counter.

Do you see what I mean?

--

Messages.Author: Tom Wylie
Messages.Body:
Alec Habig <ahabig@bigbang.astro.indiana.edu> wrote:
>>***: The others are correct.  Because it has the (D) symbol, you can
>>   :actually bleed people who aren't your prey. 
>This is rather weird.  Why, then would Night Moves have to state "bleed your
>predator or prey", since it's already a (D) card?

To restrict its effect.  Normally you could bleed *anyone* with a <D> card;
Night Moves is limiting that to two other players.  Basically a game balance
decision.

>Wish they'd post these revised rules, as the current set is rather explicit.
>A (D) action is simply one which only the affected Methusalah's minions can
>block.  It doesn't give one some special power to "direct" the action at some
>target one normally can't.  And one can only do a bleed at one's prey.

Well, actually, <D> bleeds such as Computer Hacking do allow you to bleed
anyone you want.  The rules for directed actions override the rules about
who you can bleed.

Messages.Author: Brian Wilson
Messages.Body:
Before I could do anything to stop it, Tom Wylie wrote:

> Well, actually, <D> bleeds such as Computer Hacking do allow you to bleed
> anyone you want.  The rules for directed actions override the rules about
> who you can bleed.


This doesn't read right to me. I just got my updated rules in the mail, 
and in section 13.3.1 (Who May Block Whom), when it describes Directed 
Actions, it says:

"The only directed actions that do not require a card are bleeding and
encountering another Methuselah's vampire in torpor."

By your interpretation, since Bleeding is a (D) action, I should be able
to Bleed anyone I want. Fact is, I can't - I can *only* bleed my prey.
Computer Hacking says "(D) Bleed at +1." This just sounds like a bonus on
your Bleed, which is normally at +0. Night Moves is more specific as it
says "(D) Bleed your predator or prey at +3 stealth." Clearly this is a
rules override. Govern the Unaligned and Legal Manipulation also allow
(D) Bleed actions. Now I can bleed anyone I want? These look like 
modifiers to the normal Bleed action.

I also have one card (can't find it right now - perhaps someone can fill in
the blanks for me) the specifically says you can Bleed any Methuselah in 
the game. What's the point of this text if a (D) action lets you bleed 
anyone you want anyway?

Maybe this is covered in one of the Random Rulings (I haven't been able to
stay up to date on those), but it seems odd to me. Bleed is Bleed and
affects your prey unless a card says you can bleed another Methuselah.
Otherwise, enough of these cards and we get the kind of free-for-all 
Richard Garfield was trying to avoid with the predator/prey relationship.

Messages.Author: Tom Wylie
Messages.Body:
Brian Wilson <bwilson@gate.net> wrote:
>> Well, actually, <D> bleeds such as Computer Hacking do allow you to bleed
>> anyone you want.  The rules for directed actions override the rules about
>> who you can bleed.
>This doesn't read right to me. I just got my updated rules in the mail, 
>and in section 13.3.1 (Who May Block Whom), when it describes Directed 
>Actions, it says:
>"The only directed actions that do not require a card are bleeding and
>encountering another Methuselah's vampire in torpor."

If you bleed sans a card, then you can only bleed your prey, and that
action is direction.  If you're using an action card to bleed, then the
rules for directed actions take precedence, and you can bleed anyone
you want (unless the card constrains you somehow).  Specifically, you
*can* use Computer Hacking to bleed anyone you want, because the rules
for directed action take precedence.  You can only use Night Moves to
bleed your predator or prey, since the card text takes precedence.

>I also have one card (can't find it right now - perhaps someone can fill in
>the blanks for me) the specifically says you can Bleed any Methuselah in 
>the game. What's the point of this text if a (D) action lets you bleed 
>anyone you want anyway?

Cat Burglary is a little redundant, yes.

>Otherwise, enough of these cards and we get the kind of free-for-all 
>Richard Garfield was trying to avoid with the predator/prey relationship.

Well, the final decision that you can use Computer Hacking and such to
bleed anyone you want come out of a meeting at which Richard was
in attendance.
